<title>More protein in your breakfast or snacks won’t give you more muscle without more work – a biologist separates the science from the marketing</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754402/original/file-20260817-60-i735wl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Do you really need all those protein supplements in your diet?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/protein-powder-wellness-concept-royalty-free-image/1760776823">Djavan Rodriguez/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Growing up, my brothers were fascinated by the first “Rocky” movie. They were trying to get stronger and excel in sports, so one scene stood out almost as much as Rocky sprinting up the museum steps: Before sunrise, Rocky cracked raw eggs into a glass and drank them.</p>

<p>To a teenager, this raised some questions. Why raw eggs? Was this what you needed to build muscle and become stronger? Curiosity eventually won, but one gulp was enough. The drink was as nasty as it looked. The scene was as much about showing Rocky’s toughness as it was about making a protein-rich drink to become stronger.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9DfnpaZV6vs?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Drinking five raw eggs is itself a test of strength.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Today, Rocky’s raw eggs have been replaced by protein shakes, bars and protein-enhanced everything. Grocery shelves are filled with protein-enriched cereal, pasta, chips, coffee, bread and even <a href="https://www.delish.com/food-news/a69240309/protein-pop-tarts-review/">protein-fortified Pop-Tarts</a>. When a breakfast pastry known mainly for sweetness and convenience is marketed as a protein source, it is clear that food companies are <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/22/protein-craze-general-mills-pepsico-kraft-heinz.html">capitalizing on consumers’ growing interest in protein</a>.</p>

<p>As a researcher who <a href="https://biology.richmond.edu/faculty/lboland/">studies proteins essential for nerve and muscle</a> cell function, I am accustomed to thinking about what scientific evidence actually shows. There is good science around much of the current enthusiasm for protein. But many people are already getting adequate amounts of protein in their diet. </p>

<p>So as someone also approaching the protein mania as a health-conscious consumer, I believe it’s also important to separate the marketing push to add protein to everything from what is really necessary for good health.</p>

<h2>What are proteins?</h2>

<p>Along with carbohydrates and fats, protein is one of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-are-macros-an-exercise-and-nutrition-scientist-explains-244265">three macronutrients</a> you need to eat in adequate amounts for your body to function. Carbohydrates and fats are your major sources of energy. While protein can also be used for energy, its main purpose is building and repairing the body.</p>

<p>Protein is necessary to build and sustain muscles. This includes the skeletal muscles that Rocky uses to sprint and box, the muscles that allow your heart to beat, the muscles that squeeze food through your stomach and intestines, and the muscles that open up your airways to breathe. </p>

<p>But muscle is not the only body part that needs protein. Protein is also <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/understanding/howgeneswork/protein/">important for the functioning</a> of your nervous system, immune system, skin, hormones and other essential components. </p>

<p>So protein is not just “muscle food.” It is needed throughout your body, even though the marketing of protein-rich foods focuses on muscle.  </p>

<h2>What are amino acids?</h2>

<p>Proteins are made of <a href="https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Amino-Acids">amino acids</a>, of which there are 20 types. It’s the combination and number of amino acids, as well as the <a href="https://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/protein-structure-14122136/">shapes of the proteins</a> they create, that give proteins different roles in the body. </p>

<p>Your body obtains amino acids by digesting the proteins you eat and breaking them down into these individual building blocks. How well your body absorbs amino acids and makes them available for use is affected by many factors, including the protein source and cooking. Animal proteins are generally <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/foods13111771">more digestible</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuae176">than plant proteins</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10408398.2019.1688249">cooking generally enhances</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1541-4337.12802">protein digestibility</a>. So, while Rocky’s raw eggs provided a source of protein, scrambled eggs are easier to digest and may have been a better choice. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Chart with the chemical structures of 20 amino acids" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754407/original/file-20260817-50-nqgt8q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Twenty amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.compoundchem.com/2014/09/16/aminoacids/">Andy Brunning/Compound Interest</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/">CC BY-NC-ND</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Of the 20 different amino acids in proteins, nine are considered essential because the human body cannot make them directly and must obtain them from food. Most protein-containing foods have the majority of these essential amino acids, but some foods are low in one or more of them. <a href="https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/essential-amino-acids">Animal-based proteins</a>, such as eggs, dairy, fish, poultry and lean meats, are good sources of the essential amino acids. Most <a href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/13-of-the-best-vegetarian-and-vegan-protein-sources">protein-rich plant foods</a>, such as most beans, nuts and rice, are low in one or more essential amino acids. <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19145965/">Soybeans are an exception</a>, providing a complete composition of essential amino acids. </p>

<p>Medical professionals recommend <a href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/do-i-need-to-worry-about-eating-complete-proteins">eating a variety of protein sources</a>, including some that are complete, to ensure you’re getting all of the essential amino acids. Eating a mixture of protein-rich plant foods can overcome deficiencies in one particular plant food. </p>

<p>Protein powders, often used as supplements, vary in essential amino acid content and composition. Compared to animal-based powders, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00726-018-2640-5">plant-based powders</a> tend to have lower levels of one or more essential amino acids and lower protein levels in total. </p>

<h2>How much protein do you need?</h2>

<p>There is little scientific debate that dietary protein is critical to good health. A harder calculation is how much protein you need.</p>

<p>A commonly cited standard is the federal <a href="https://theconversation.com/nutrition-facts-labels-have-a-complicated-legacy-a-historian-explains-the-science-and-politics-of-translating-food-into-information-231894">recommended dietary allowance, or RDA</a>. In January 2026, the U.S. government <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/white-house-releases-new-dietary-guidelines-encouraging-americans/story?id=128976128">raised the adult RDA of dietary protein</a> from 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight to 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram. For a 150-pound person, this almost <a href="https://cdn.realfood.gov/DGA.pdf">doubles the recommendation</a> from 54 grams to between 80 to 110 grams a day. Some experts have interpreted this update as focusing on optimizing health as opposed to <a href="https://clinicalnutritionreport.com/articles/protein-per-kilogram-2026-position-stand/">ensuring adequate protein intake</a> to avoid deficiency.</p>

<p>The new federal guidelines are <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/why-nutrition-experts-are-wary-of-new-federal-dietary-guidelines-that-advise-doubling-protein">not without controversy</a>, however. How much <a href="https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2026/03/how-much-protein.html">protein a given person needs</a> is a complex question that depends on individual health goals, age, sex, activity level, medical history and other factors. Consulting with a medical provider or licensed nutritionist can help individualize dietary protein targets.</p>

<p>Many experts agree that the <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-03632-1">average, healthy U.S. adult</a> <a href="https://healthcare.utah.edu/healthfeed/2026/07/protein-foods-are-everywhere-right-now-do-you-actually-need-more-protein">already consumes</a> <a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/protein-boosted-foods-are-everywhere-now-but-do-we-actually-need-more-protein/">enough protein</a>. While most healthy adults can tolerate moderately high protein intake, overloading on protein <a href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/can-you-eat-too-much-protein">could create health problems</a>, such as kidney damage and digestive issues.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Person placing package of steak into grocery cart" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754415/original/file-20260817-50-qm4zla.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Most Americans don’t need to worry about getting enough protein in their diet.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Companies market high-protein diets to encourage weight loss because consuming more protein tends to <a href="https://theconversation.com/im-trying-to-lose-weight-and-eat-healthily-why-do-i-feel-so-hungry-all-the-time-what-can-i-do-about-it-215808">increase feelings of fullness</a>. A 2026 study identified a link between the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2026.03.017">amino acid leucine</a> and appetite suppression through a connection between the gut and the brain. </p>

<p>That said, while suppressing appetite may help with weight loss, it may also reduce a person’s consumption of calories from fruits, vegetables, beans and whole grains that <a href="https://theconversation.com/fiber-is-your-bodys-natural-guide-to-weight-management-rather-than-cutting-carbs-out-of-your-diet-eat-them-in-their-original-fiber-packaging-instead-205159">provide fiber</a>, vitamins and other important nutrients. </p>

<h2>What about protein powders and supplements?</h2>

<p>Protein powders are a <a href="https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/protein-powder-market">US$20 billion industry</a>, and their popularity reflects both the idea that dietary proteins can support muscle growth and <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-diet-can-help-prevent-muscle-injuries-in-over-50s-257649">reduce muscle loss</a> as well as how <a href="https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/u-s-protein-supplements-market-107171">lucrative protein supplements</a> can be.  </p>

<p>For people with low appetites or those who have <a href="https://www.uclahealth.org/news/article/are-you-getting-enough-protein-heres-what-happens-if-you-dont">difficulty meeting</a> <a href="https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2026/03/how-much-protein.html">dietary protein recommendations</a>, protein-enriched foods can be a useful way to increase protein intake. This might include those taking <a href="https://theconversation.com/youve-reached-your-weight-loss-goal-on-glp-1-medications-what-now-270413">GLP-1 weight loss medications</a>, which can reduce appetite and make it <a href="https://www.uchealth.org/today/nutrition-vital-when-taking-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs/">harder to eat enough protein and other nutrients</a>. </p>

<p>But while a protein shake can deliver essential amino acids, it does not provide the <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/the-scoop-on-protein-powder-2020030918986">broader nutritional value</a> of protein-rich foods, such as fish, beans, nuts, yogurt and soy products. Moreover, protein-fortified packaged foods may come with increased sugar, salt or saturated fats. A protein bar may be closer to a candy bar with better branding. </p>

<p>For these reasons, medical organizations recommend consuming well-planned <a href="https://www.kidney.org/news-protein-our-diet-variety-and-moderation-key">combinations of protein sources</a> <a href="https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/healthy-eating/eat-smart/nutrition-basics/aha-diet-and-lifestyle-recommendations">from nonpackaged foods</a>. </p>

<h2>Building muscle takes more than just protein</h2>

<p>Beyond bodybuilding, science has elevated society’s appreciation for the importance of dietary protein in combating <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/nu17152461">muscle loss</a> <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/healthy-aging-and-longevity/muscle-loss-and-protein-needs-in-older-adults">due to aging</a>, weight loss or injury.</p>

<p>Some experts don’t think doubling protein intake is as important to building muscle as <a href="https://theconversation.com/resistance-exercise-is-far-from-futile-the-unheralded-benefits-of-weight-training-220269">resistance training</a>, a type of exercise that creates force and strain on muscles to signal the body to repair and grow more muscle. This is different from endurance training that improves aerobic capacity. </p>

<p>A 2021 clinical trial found that only when dietary protein was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/nqaa372">combined with heavy resistance training</a> did older adults see improved muscle size, strength and function.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Person reaching towards dumbbells on a rack" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754418/original/file-20260817-50-no9s5b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Resistance training is essential to building and strengthening muscles.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/hands-of-mixed-race-woman-reaching-for-dumbbells-royalty-free-image/700712501">JGI/Tom Grill/Tetra Images via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Eating more protein alone will not build muscle because the critical <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s42255-025-01298-7">molecular pathways</a> for muscle growth and strength require repeatedly placing heavy forces on the muscle. Challenging your muscles with <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare11172443">repeated training and progressively heavier weights</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00613.2016">stimulates muscles to adapt</a> by becoming larger and better able to produce force. The nervous system adapts too, becoming better able to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-023-05201-8">activate and coordinate muscle movement</a>. </p>

<p>Resistance training is also key to preventing the muscle loss that accompanies weight loss from <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/watch/glp-1-diet">GLP-1 medications</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/steep-physical-decline-with-age-is-not-inevitable-heres-how-strength-training-can-change-the-trajectory-213131">aging</a> and <a href="http://doi.org/10.4085/1062-6050-550-19">recovering from injury</a>. The key takeaway is that dietary protein and resistance training <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-022-00508-w">work together</a> to promote muscle growth and maintain strength.</p>

<p>Rocky knew that drinking the eggs wasn’t enough – he still had to challenge his muscles to build muscle and strength.</p>

<h2>Protein in everything: Science vs. sales pitch</h2>

<p>So, is the protein craze based on real science, or is it a fad?</p>

<p>It’s both. The science is clear – dietary protein supports muscle maintenance, growth, injury repair and recovery, fullness and weight regulation, and healthy aging. The fad is the idea that any food with added protein is automatically better – and that you can always benefit from more protein.</p>

<p>Protein deserves attention. But the marketing of protein-fortified food products is not a shortcut to a quality diet that provides a complete source of amino acids from nutritious foods.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287942/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Do you really need all those protein supplements in your diet? Djavan Rodriguez/Moment via Getty Images Growing up, my brothers were fascinated by the first “Rocky” movie
They were trying to get stronger and excel in sports, so one scene stood out almost as much as Rocky sprinting up the museum steps: Before sunrise, Rocky cracked raw eggs into a glass and drank them
To a teenager, this raised some questions
Why raw eggs? Was this what you needed to build muscle and become stronger? Curiosity eventually won, but one gulp was enough
The scene was as much about showing Rocky’s toughness as it was about making a protein-rich drink to become stronger
Drinking five raw eggs is itself a test of strength
Today, Rocky’s raw eggs have been replaced by protein shakes, bars and protein-enhanced everything
Grocery shelves are filled with protein-enriched cereal, pasta, chips, coffee, bread and even protein-fortified Pop-Tarts
When a breakfast pastry known mainly for sweetness and convenience is marketed as a protein source, it is clear that food companies are capitalizing on consumers’ growing interest in protein
As a researcher who studies proteins essential for nerve and muscle cell function, I am accustomed to thinking about what scientific evidence actually shows
There is good science around much of the current enthusiasm for protein
But many people are already getting adequate amounts of protein in their diet

So as someone also approaching the protein mania as a health-conscious consumer, I believe it’s also important to separate the marketing push to add protein to everything from what is really necessary for good health
What are proteins? Along with carbohydrates and fats, protein is one of the three macronutrients you need to eat in adequate amounts for your body to function
Carbohydrates and fats are your major sources of energy
While protein can also be used for energy, its main purpose is building and repairing the body
Protein is necessary to build and sustain muscles

This includes the skeletal muscles that Rocky uses to sprint and box, the muscles that allow your heart to beat, the muscles that squeeze food through your stomach and intestines, and the muscles that open up your airways to breathe
But muscle is not the only body part that needs protein
Protein is also important for the functioning of your nervous system, immune system, skin, hormones and other essential components
So protein is not just “muscle food.” It is needed throughout your body, even though the marketing of protein-rich foods focuses on muscle
What are amino acids? Proteins are made of amino acids , of which there are 20 types
It’s the combination and number of amino acids, as well as the shapes of the proteins they create, that give proteins different roles in the body
Your body obtains amino acids by digesting the proteins you eat and breaking them down into these individual building blocks
How well your body absorbs amino acids and makes them available for use is affected by many factors, including the protein source and cooking
Animal proteins are generally more digestible than plant proteins , and cooking generally enhances protein digestibility
So, while Rocky’s raw eggs provided a source of protein, scrambled eggs are easier to digest and may have been a better choice
Twenty amino acids are the building blocks of proteins

Andy Brunning/Compound Interest , CC BY-NC-ND Of the 20 different amino acids in proteins, nine are considered essential because the human body cannot make them directly and must obtain them from food
Most protein-containing foods have the majority of these essential amino acids, but some foods are low in one or more of them
Animal-based proteins , such as eggs, dairy, fish, poultry and lean meats, are good sources of the essential amino acids
Most protein-rich plant foods , such as most beans, nuts and rice, are low in one or more essential amino acids
Soybeans are an exception , providing a complete composition of essential amino acids
Medical professionals recommend eating a variety of protein sources , including some that are complete, to ensure you’re getting all of the essential amino acids
Eating a mixture of protein-rich plant foods can overcome deficiencies in one particular plant food
Protein powders, often used as supplements, vary in essential amino acid content and composition
Compared to animal-based powders, plant-based powders tend to have lower levels of one or more essential amino acids and lower protein levels in total

<title>The importance of teaching students what AI can’t do</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754978/original/file-20260819-50-terihh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1720%2C3159%2C2106&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Emile Bernard&#39;s &#39;Madeleine in the Bois d&#39;Amour&#39; (1888).</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/madeleine-in-the-bois-damour-1888-from-the-collection-of-news-photo/1151163973?adppopup=true">Art Media/The Print Collector via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It’s disconcerting to envision human thought becoming redundant or deemed inferior due to advancements in artificial intelligence. But for all its ills, AI cannot be ignored or wished away. It’s here to stay, and I want my students to understand the stakes of becoming too reliant on this technology.</p>

<p>I can’t blame them for wondering why they should dedicate so much time and effort to <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/college-confidential/202508/why-human-writing-is-essential-in-the-age-of-ai">honing their writing</a> and critical thinking skills if large language models appear to do a passable job.</p>

<p>Yet this situation has major implications for culture and societies. </p>

<p>It’s easy to envision a future where AI dependency leads to intellectual conformity and the erosion of critical thinking. Researchers <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-induced-cultural-stagnation-is-no-longer-speculation-its-already-happening-272488">are already documenting these effects</a>, which threaten to render the <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/timbajarin/2026/07/21/the-quiet-death-of-critical-thinking-in-the-age-of-ai-summaries/">hard work of wrestling with ideas a lost art</a>.</p>

<p>This is why I think it’s critical for educators to confront AI head-on. The key, I believe, is teaching students to distinguish <a href="https://pe.gatech.edu/blog/industry-trends/ai-and-data-science">AI’s pattern recognition skills</a> from its inability to daydream, inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself.</p>

<h2>Tell me what you think</h2>

<p>In a course I recently taught on Southern Gothic literature, I gave my students an exercise. They were tasked with prompting AI to analyze the “emotional atmosphere” of a scene from Carson McCullers’ 1940 novel “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/heart-is-a-lonely-hunter-carson-mccullers?variant=39973876301858">The Heart is a Lonely Hunter</a>.”</p>

<p>Many of the characters readers meet in <a href="https://www.uncannymagazine.com/article/southern-gothic-shadows-superstition-and-the-supernatural/">Southern Gothic works</a> like McCullers’ are freakish and brutal. Rendered from a distorted, unnatural lens, they speak in odd dialects and conjure what <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2025/mar/25/so-much-more-than-southern-gothic-flannery-oconnor-at-100">Flannery O’Connor</a> called the “<a href="https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/03/25/flannery-o-connor-grotesque-reading/">grotesque</a>.” They live in isolated places that are stuck in the past and, to use another term of O'Connor’s, are “<a href="https://www.nightmare-magazine.com/nonfiction/the-h-word-the-dirty-south/">Christ-haunted</a>.” </p>

<p>Many readers have difficulty synthesizing the strange worlds of these characters. AI has an even harder time generalizing the complex tensions between faith and unbelief, or good and evil, that animate these stories.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Black and white photo of a young woman sitting a stoop, resting her head in one hand while cradling a cigarette in the other." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Carson McCullers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Carson%20McCullers/c1f89f8c33814555ac3ca8e8e1bc8122/photo">AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>To limit the range of responses and allow useful comparisons, I provided students with scenes involving the main characters of the novel. One of them was the heartrending sequence in which Spiros Antonapoulos, a deaf character, is sent away to a state insane asylum, leaving his only friend, John Singer, behind.</p>

<p>The scene carries a palpable sense of dread and sadness. Further, it invokes righteous anger toward Antonapoulos’ cousin for sending him away – a decision driven by convenience and based on a misunderstanding of Spiros’ struggles as deviant, antisocial behavior. That he is from an immigrant background living in small-town Georgia gives the scene an even sharper edge.</p>

<p>ChatGPT, however, rendered the scene using sterile, abstract terminology. To pull a representative response that one of my students shared: “The atmosphere is devastatingly lonely and suspended in time. The scene feels quiet, helpless and emotionally one-sided. There is no dramatic farewell; instead, the moment is marked by Singer’s silent anguish. The train’s departure symbolizes irreversible separation.”</p>

<p>The assessment is clinical and cold. It fails to capture the weight of deep sadness that exudes from the separation of two friends who have only each other. It included a factual mistake, too: It’s a bus, not a train, that pulls away.</p>

<p>Also missing is any clear acknowledgment of Singer’s fear for the horrors in store for Antonapoulos, and the dramatic irony created by Antonapoulos’ own seeming obliviousness to how his life is being upended. AI simply lacks the lived experience to become <a href="https://sbmi.uth.edu/blog/2024/artificial-intelligence-versus-human-intelligence.htm">contextually aware</a> in ways that allow it to truly understand McCullers’ haunting novel.</p>

<p>Because AI largely functions as an <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/joetoscano1/2025/09/03/ai-is-destroying-seo-rank-now-requires-answer-engine-optimization/">optimization engine</a> – relying on synthesizing vast amounts of online data and summarizing the results – its analyses of this scene and others were consistently shallow; they “lacked depth” and were filled with “vague platitudes,” as two students put it. </p>

<h2>Accessing the embodied experience</h2>

<p>Next, I asked my students to have AI generate “a new scene involving at least three characters” of their choosing.</p>

<p>The creative output was even more soulless. Students were especially amused that AI had John Singer, who acts as a hub connecting all the other characters, speaking on a variety of subjects. The problem, of course, is that Singer, like Antonapoulos, is also deaf. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

            </figcaption>

<p>That AI could not fathom the experience of being unable to hear isn’t surprising. It’s important to remember that engaging with AI means dealing with a <a href="https://www.sainsburywellcome.org/blog/ai-embodiment-and-neuroscience">synthetic intelligence</a> that lacks a body through which to experience and interact with the world.</p>

<p>Without an embodied presence it cannot put itself in the shoes of its users and experience anything approaching human empathy. While tech billionaires such as Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen may <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/04/opinion/empathy-ethics.html">see empathy and introspection as weaknesses</a>, those traits are the beating heart of literature and art, the wellspring of creativity and human connection.</p>

<p>In other words, emotion, empathy and irrationality could be seen as some of the most powerful counterweights to AI.</p>

<p></p>

<h2>Embracing human frailty</h2>

<p>There may be situations where AI may be useful to my students, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h4NAygTNago">and I think efforts to ban the use of AI</a> are unfeasible and counterproductive. </p>

<p>The ability to forgo these tools altogether is largely a luxury. Just as many people can’t afford to have someone else clean their homes, landscape their yards or nanny their kids, those struggling to make ends meet <a href="https://www.cgdev.org/blog/how-do-poorest-use-ai">may need to lean on AI assistance</a>.</p>

<p>But my hope is that my students – especially when it comes to their intellectual work – will understand that deploying the technology requires abandoning capacities that are essential to human thought and creativity: imagination, intuition and self-reflection.</p>

<p>I want them to think twice before trying to mask, with a chatbot, the inherent frailties, weaknesses, obsessions and digressions of the human mind. Instead, I want them to embrace these human tendencies and surrender to what poet William Wordsworth called the “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/91748/william-wordsworth-101">spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings</a>.” </p>

<p>After all, the greatest art often emerges from those who are at their most vulnerable, confused and lost.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/286100/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Art Media/The Print Collector via Getty Images It’s disconcerting to envision human thought becoming redundant or deemed inferior due to advancements in artificial intelligence
But for all its ills, AI cannot be ignored or wished away
It’s here to stay, and I want my students to understand the stakes of becoming too reliant on this technology
I can’t blame them for wondering why they should dedicate so much time and effort to honing their writing and critical thinking skills if large language models appear to do a passable job
Yet this situation has major implications for culture and societies
It’s easy to envision a future where AI dependency leads to intellectual conformity and the erosion of critical thinking
Researchers are already documenting these effects , which threaten to render the hard work of wrestling with ideas a lost art
This is why I think it’s critical for educators to confront AI head-on
The key, I believe, is teaching students to distinguish AI’s pattern recognition skills from its inability to daydream, inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself
Tell me what you think In a course I recently taught on Southern Gothic literature, I gave my students an exercise

They were tasked with prompting AI to analyze the “emotional atmosphere” of a scene from Carson McCullers’ 1940 novel “ The Heart is a Lonely Hunter .” Many of the characters readers meet in Southern Gothic works like McCullers’ are freakish and brutal

Rendered from a distorted, unnatural lens, they speak in odd dialects and conjure what Flannery O’Connor called the “ grotesque .” They live in isolated places that are stuck in the past and, to use another term of O'Connor’s, are “ Christ-haunted .” Many readers have difficulty synthesizing the strange worlds of these characters
AI has an even harder time generalizing the complex tensions between faith and unbelief, or good and evil, that animate these stories

One of them was the heartrending sequence in which Spiros Antonapoulos, a deaf character, is sent away to a state insane asylum, leaving his only friend, John Singer, behind
The scene carries a palpable sense of dread and sadness

That he is from an immigrant background living in small-town Georgia gives the scene an even sharper edge
ChatGPT, however, rendered the scene using sterile, abstract terminology
To pull a representative response that one of my students shared: “The atmosphere is devastatingly lonely and suspended in time
The scene feels quiet, helpless and emotionally one-sided
There is no dramatic farewell; instead, the moment is marked by Singer’s silent anguish

It included a factual mistake, too: It’s a bus, not a train, that pulls away

<title>Antarctic krill fishing is now concentrated in the exact pattern conservation rules were designed to prevent</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754898/original/file-20260819-50-428t87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C4240%2C2826&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A trawler fishes for krill in the Southern Ocean.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/OceanFisheriesAntarcticKrillFishing/9fdace78c0754781ac681bc427f23cf6/photo">AP Photo/David Keyton</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The companies fishing for Antarctic krill have harvested so much so quickly that the <a href="https://thefishsite.com/articles/antarctic-krill-fishery-closes-for-2026">season had to close</a> in August 2026, three months before it was scheduled to end. That’s the second consecutive year of an early closing.</p>

<p>The fishing industry has said these developments are evidence that the management system is <a href="https://www.akerbiomarine.com/news/the-antarctic-krill-fishery-closes-for-2026-as-precautionary-management-measures-take-effect">working as intended</a>: Once the 620,000-ton limit, called a “trigger level,” is reached, fishing must stop. And the evidence indicates that the <a href="https://www.theqrillcompany.com/blog-and-news/antarctic-krill-fishery-set-to-close-this-week">krill fishing boats do stop</a> when the trigger level is hit.</p>

<p>However, as <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Taryx5kAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">someone who has been studying</a> <a href="https://www.krillseekerlab.com/">Antarctic krill ecology</a> and their role in the Southern Ocean ecosystem for 16 years, what currently concerns me most is how locally concentrated that harvest has become. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Krill are tiny, but they are a vital part of the Southern Ocean’s ecosystem.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nsf.gov/science-matters/antarctic-krill-superheroes-southern-ocean">Dan Costa/National Science Foundation</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A key species for Antarctic marine ecosystems</h2>

<p><a href="https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Euphausia_superba/">Antarctic krill, <em>Euphausia superba</em></a>, is a principal food source for penguins, seals, whales, seabirds and fish. But krill are not distributed evenly across the Southern Ocean: They gather in dense, patchy groups in particular locations. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsr.2008.12.007">They are most numerous</a> in the waters off the Antarctic Peninsula stretching into the Scotia Sea.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecss.2026.109925">Breeding penguins</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15828">and seals</a> depend on high concentrations of krill found relatively close to their colonies because they must repeatedly return to those colonies to feed their young. If they don’t find krill nearby, they can’t go much farther into the ocean to seek alternative prey without risking their young starving on the shore. More than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-59223-9">30 years of observations</a> from the Antarctic Peninsula show why this concentration of krill matters. Models using those observations predict overall penguin performance – factors such as breeding success and foraging trip duration – to decline when fishing removes a high proportion of the krill available locally.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsr.2022.103867">Baleen whales</a> are more mobile, but they depend on exceptionally <a href="https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/214/1/131/10226/Mechanics-hydrodynamics-and-energetics-of-blue">dense krill patches to make feeding worthwhile</a> and often congregate in the same productive hot spots. There is growing concern around the overlap between the krill fishery and important feeding grounds of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51954-x">recovering fin whale population</a>.</p>

<p>Perhaps obviously, those locations are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2417203122">also attractive to fishing vessels</a>, because it’s most efficient to catch large amounts of krill in those places. Krill meal is used as feed for aquaculture, pets and ornamental fish, among others. While some nations use krill meal as an additional food source for their people, human use of krill products is primarily through <a href="https://www.webmd.com/vitamins-supplements/krill-oil">dietary supplements</a> containing oils that are extracted from krill.</p>

<h2>Efforts to manage fishing</h2>

<p>An intergovernmental agency called the <a href="https://www.ccamlr.org/">Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources</a>, better known by its acronym CCAMLR, manages the Antarctic krill fishery, among other sea life in the Southern Ocean. It was created in 1982 amid concern that the rapidly expanding krill fishery could remove too much food from penguins, seals, whales and other predators. At present, <a href="https://www.ccamlr.org/en/organisation/members">26 countries and the European Union</a> are members of the commission.</p>

<p>In 1991 the commission set a precautionary threshold of 620,000 tons on the annual catch of krill across a region known as Area 48, which extends from the Antarctic Peninsula across the Scotia Sea. CCAMLR refers to this threshold as the “trigger level” because reaching it was intended to trigger a management system splitting the region into smaller areas, with their own specific catch limits, before catches could increase further.</p>

<p>The commission recognized that catching even a relatively small amount of krill could damage local ecosystems if it all came from a small area. In 2009, it placed <a href="https://cm.ccamlr.org/measure-51-07-2022">regional caps</a> within the 620,000-ton trigger level, limiting how much could be taken from each of four subareas within the broader Area 48: the Antarctic Peninsula, the South Orkney Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.</p>

<p><iframe id="LxTZu" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LxTZu/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the region of the Southern Ocean below and east of South America, toward the Antarctic Peninsula and the Scotia Sea."></iframe></p>

<h2>Regional caps expire</h2>

<p>While the regional caps were in effect, krill fishing ran the full year without ever hitting the trigger level.</p>

<p>The conservation measure that established the regional caps <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpol.2025.106787">expired in 2024</a>, and was not renewed or replaced. The trigger level remains in force, but companies are now allowed to fish for krill in whichever krill-rich areas they find most productive.</p>

<p>In each of the two seasons since then, fishing companies have <a href="https://oceanographicmagazine.com/news/antarctic-krill-fishery-shuts-early-for-second-year-running/">hit the 620,000-ton trigger level</a> months before the end of the season, in part by focusing their efforts on places where they can catch the most krill.</p>

<p>Global Fishing Watch’s <a href="https://globalfishingwatch.org/platform/map">vessel tracking</a> shows that in 2026 the krill fishing fleet operated primarily in the Bransfield and Gerlache straits of the Antarctic Peninsula and northwest of the South Orkney Islands, with little to no fishing in the rest of Area 48.</p>

<p>Krill fishing is now happening in precisely the concentrated pattern the regional-cap conservation measure was created to prevent.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>An opportunity</h2>

<p>The concentration of fishing comes as the overall ecosystem is becoming more vulnerable as a result of climate change. The Antarctic Peninsula and Scotia Sea are among the <a href="https://geographical.co.uk/climate-change/the-worlds-five-fastest-warming-regions">fastest-warming places on the planet</a>.</p>

<p>Decreased sea ice cover, changing wind patterns and warming ocean temperatures are already <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2020.615214">altering krill habitat</a> and the Southern Ocean food web. A long-term analysis of the Antarctic krill population in this region found that their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-018-0370-z">densities declined by about 59%</a> between the late 20th century and more recent decades, with the sharpest declines in the northern part of their range.</p>

<p>Because of the rapid changes to the marine environment of the Antarctic Peninsula and the region’s exceptional ecological importance, <a href="https://cancilleria.gob.ar/en/argentina-and-chile-presented-proposal-marine-protected-area-antarctic-peninsula-again">Argentina and Chile have proposed a marine protected area</a> to conserve important habitats, biodiversity and ecological processes. The proposal, developed through years of scientific planning, would also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpol.2019.103720">protect areas important to krill and the predators that depend on them</a>. But eight years after it was formally submitted to CCAMLR, member nations have still not reached the consensus required to adopt it.</p>

<p>The CCAMLR members next <a href="https://meetings.ccamlr.org/en">meet in October 2026</a>. At that meeting, members need to restore binding spatial limits on krill catches while agreeing on a more sophisticated ecosystem-based management system that distributes fishing at scales relevant to krill and their predators. The proposed marine protected area will also be up for discussion, again. The concerns that led to the committee being created 44 years ago – fears about krill fishing harming krill-dependent Antarctic wildlife – have not diminished over the decades.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290019/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The commission recognized that catching even a relatively small amount of krill could damage local ecosystems if it all came from a small area

In 2009, it placed regional caps within the 620,000-ton trigger level, limiting how much could be taken from each of four subareas within the broader Area 48: the Antarctic Peninsula, the South Orkney Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands
Regional caps expire While the regional caps were in effect, krill fishing ran the full year without ever hitting the trigger level
The conservation measure that established the regional caps expired in 2024 , and was not renewed or replaced
The trigger level remains in force, but companies are now allowed to fish for krill in whichever krill-rich areas they find most productive

In each of the two seasons since then, fishing companies have hit the 620,000-ton trigger level months before the end of the season, in part by focusing their efforts on places where they can catch the most krill

Global Fishing Watch’s vessel tracking shows that in 2026 the krill fishing fleet operated primarily in the Bransfield and Gerlache straits of the Antarctic Peninsula and northwest of the South Orkney Islands, with little to no fishing in the rest of Area 48
Krill fishing is now happening in precisely the concentrated pattern the regional-cap conservation measure was created to prevent
Krill fishing under regional limits, seen on the left, was much more widespread than after the regional limits were lifted, seen on the right
Bernard with data from CCAMLR and Global Fishing Watch , CC BY-ND An opportunity The concentration of fishing comes as the overall ecosystem is becoming more vulnerable as a result of climate change
The Antarctic Peninsula and Scotia Sea are among the fastest-warming places on the planet
Decreased sea ice cover, changing wind patterns and warming ocean temperatures are already altering krill habitat and the Southern Ocean food web

A long-term analysis of the Antarctic krill population in this region found that their densities declined by about 59% between the late 20th century and more recent decades, with the sharpest declines in the northern part of their range

Because of the rapid changes to the marine environment of the Antarctic Peninsula and the region’s exceptional ecological importance, Argentina and Chile have proposed a marine protected area to conserve important habitats, biodiversity and ecological processes
The proposal, developed through years of scientific planning, would also protect areas important to krill and the predators that depend on them
But eight years after it was formally submitted to CCAMLR, member nations have still not reached the consensus required to adopt it

<title>A seemingly technical change to international student visas could disrupt teaching and research at US universities</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755276/original/file-20260820-50-stfb0r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6668%2C4445&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">New visa changes for international students are the latest step the Trump administration has taken that can make it harder for students to come to the U.S. to complete their degrees. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/international-graduates-traveling-for-global-royalty-free-illustration/2273210661?phrase=international%20students%20US&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">LVector/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The Trump administration is revising <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/16/trump-administration-issues-final-rule-end-foreign-student-visa-abuse">a visa rule</a> for international students that in part determines how long, and under what conditions, they can stay in the country. The change sounds technical. Its effects are not.</p>

<p>Beginning Sept. 15, 2026, most students entering the U.S. on <a href="https://j1visa.state.gov/basics/other-u-s-visas/studying-at-u-s-universities-and-colleges-f-1-versus-j-1-visas/">F-1 and J-1 visas</a> – meaning visas for international students and  exchange visitors, including students and scholars – will no longer be admitted for “<a href="https://www.nafsa.org/Duration-status-explainer">duration of status</a>.” Duration of status means they can remain in the U.S. as long they are enrolled in their academic program, or shortly thereafter. </p>

<p>Now, academic visa holders will instead be able to stay in the country for a predetermined period of time, generally four years. </p>

<p>Those who need more time to complete a degree will have to reapply to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for permission to stay.</p>

<p>The change could also complicate international travel: Students returning to the U.S. will have to make sure their fixed period of admission has not expired, in addition to having the valid visa and school documents normally required for reentry.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/17/2026-14439/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">rule also lets full-time international students</a> stay 30 days in the country after they complete their program, as opposed to the 60 days they currently have to remain in the U.S. </p>

<p><a href="https://fordhampress.com/degrees-of-empire-hb-9781531514556.html">I study the history of international students in U.S. higher education</a>. Universities rely on international students for tuition, teaching, research and other kinds of skilled work. </p>

<p>These new rules will make it harder for some international students to visit and stay in the country, a result that will likely have negative consequences for universities and colleges, too. </p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man with a black robe and graduation cap stands near a group of people shouting with their hands covering their mouths." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755275/original/file-20260820-60-evw4y1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/topshot-graduating-harvard-student-victor-flores-and-others-news-photo/2216820355?adppopup=true">Rick Friedman/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>

<h2>A look at international students</h2>

<p>U.S. colleges and universities hosted <a href="https://www.iie.org/news/open-doors-2025-press-release/">1,177,766 international students in the 2024-25 school year</a>, an all-time high that made up approximately 6% of all higher education students.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.iie.org/news/open-doors-2025-press-release/">Most of them were working toward degrees in</a> in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. </p>

<p>Nearly 488,500 of those international students were seeking graduate degrees. More than 294,000 of them participated in a federal program called <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/students-and-exchange-visitors/optional-practical-training-opt-for-f-1-students">Optional Practical Training</a>, which helps some international students work in jobs related to their field of study before or after they graduate. </p>

<p><a href="https://opendoorsdata.org/data/international-students/enrollment-trends/">International enrollment grew steadily</a> at U.S. colleges and universities, from about 565,000 students in the 2004-05 school year to more than 1 million by the 2015-16 academic year.  </p>

<p>Growth then <a href="https://opendoorsdata.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Open-Doors_2010-2022.pdf?">slowed during the first Trump administration</a> but began rising again after 2021. </p>

<p>The concentration is much higher in some programs and institutions. At Purdue, for example, <a href="https://engineering.purdue.edu/ME/AboutUs?">international students make up</a> 63% of graduate students in mechanical engineering. At Columbia University, non-U.S. residents made up 53% of graduate <a href="https://opir.columbia.edu/sites/opir.columbia.edu/files/content/Columbia%20Facts/Fact_2024.pdf?">students in the fall of 2024</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.cnn.com/2024/11/20/us/china-international-students-us-decline-hnk-dst">Since 2024</a>, the greatest number of international students has <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/asian-america/indian-students-surpass-chinese-largest-international-group-rcna180783">come from India</a>. The next largest group is students from China. For more than a decade, <a href="https://www.statista.com/statistics/372900/number-of-chinese-students-that-study-in-the-us/?srsltid=AfmBOorAco_NNAH4SWV02jrhL5seBdGqN1CM7Pb3vEcjYtUAYryolGhF">students from China</a> made up the <a href="https://opendoorsdata.org/data/international-students/all-places-of-origin/?">largest group of international students</a> in the U.S. But <a href="https://www.voanews.com/a/chinese-still-largest-group-of-foreign-students-in-us/7407560.html">the number of Chinese students</a> has <a href="https://www.iie.org/news/open-doors-2025-press-release/">dropped over the past several years</a>. </p>

<p>International students are important for university finances, too. </p>

<p>Most of these students <a href="https://studentaid.gov/understand-aid/eligibility/requirements/non-us-citizens">are not eligible</a> for U.S. federal student aid or loans. </p>

<p>More <a href="https://opendoorsdata.org/fast_facts/fast-facts-2024/">than half of international students report</a> “personal or family funds” as their primary source of financial support to help pay for their education. These students <a href="https://www.iie.org/news/open-doors-2025-press-release/">contributed nearly US$55 billion</a> to the U.S. economy in 2024, according to the international student exchange nonprofit Institute of International Education.</p>

<p>International graduate students also frequently teach undergraduate courses, conduct experiments and staff research laboratories. </p>

<h2>What the rule changes</h2>

<p>Until now, most international students did not have to reapply to maintain or extend their standard F-1 student visa midway through their course of study. </p>

<p>And if a student remained enrolled and complied with immigration rules, a university could extend the student’s expected completion date of their program when more time was needed. </p>

<p>The new rule introduces a separate federal immigration review for every student whose course of study goes beyond four years. This, according to the Department of Homeland Security, will add <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/17/2026-14439/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">393,500 new visa reviews to the U.S. government workload each year</a>. </p>

<h2>Not a strict timeline</h2>

<p>Academic work does not always proceed on schedule. Research changes direction. Funding gets delayed. A dissertation needs another semester. </p>

<p>If a student reaches the end of their visa’s limits before they finish their degree, a university can still say that the student is making appropriate progress and needs more time – but now the U.S. government will also have to agree that the student can remain enrolled and stay in the country.</p>

<p>The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration is among the higher education groups that <a href="https://www.presidentsalliance.org/press/presidents-alliance-opposes-administrations-rule-ending-duration-of-status/">has warned the change could disrupt teaching and research</a>, as well as discourage students from choosing a U.S. school altogether. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/17/2026-14439/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">Department of Homeland Security has acknowledged</a> that the change may be disruptive. But the <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/17/2026-14439/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">agency argues that fixed student visa time</a> periods will give immigration officials more opportunities to check whether students are following visa requirements and to conduct national security screening.</p>

<h2>A broader campaign</h2>

<p>The first Trump administration <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/09/25/2020-20845/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">proposed a similar policy</a> in 2020. The Biden administration <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/07/06/2021-13929/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant">withdrew this visa proposal in 2021</a>. Trump then revived the proposal after returning to office. </p>

<p>This policy change comes alongside other immigration changes that make it harder for international students to attend U.S. schools. </p>

<p>In 2025, the Trump White House tried unsuccessfully to <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/06/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-restricts-foreign-student-visas-at-harvard-university/">stop Harvard from enrolling any international students</a>. <a href="https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2025/06/federal-judge-blocks-trump-plan-to-ban-international-students-at-harvard/">Federal courts blocked that measure</a> in June 2025.</p>

<p>Secretary of State Marco Rubio also announced in May 2025 that the State Department was <a href="https://www.state.gov/briefings/department-press-briefing-may-29-2025">beginning to revoke visas of some Chinese students</a> and increasing the scrutiny of prospective international students from China and Hong Kong. </p>

<p>The administration said in January 2026 that <a href="https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/News/visas-news/suspension-of-visa-issuance-to-foreign-nationals-to-protect-the-security-of-the-united-states.html">it had revoked 8,000 student visas</a> since the start of Trump’s second term. </p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/providence-rhode-island-united-states-a-graduate-stands-up-news-photo/2216368611?adppopup=true">Joseph Prezioso/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>The new rule does not end international education or impose a four-year maximum on all students’ degrees. It does mean, however, that more international students will need to get additional levels of federal approval so they can complete their education in the U.S.</p>

<p>A student in a six-year doctoral program can still finish their degree, but they will generally need federal approval to remain in the country beyond four years. A student in a two-year master’s program who finishes on schedule may never need an extension. </p>

<p>The four-year limit can also affect students whose programs are designed to take longer. The <a href="https://www.uc.edu/news/articles/2024/02/get-answers-to-all-of-your-co-op-questions.html">University of Cincinnati’s engineering degree generally takes five years to complete</a>, for example. Some medical residency and fellowship pathways for J-1 physicians routinely extend five to seven years.</p>

<p>These new roadblocks can determine whether students finish degrees, or remain with their partners and children. They can also determine whether laboratories keep researchers and employers retain graduates trained in the U.S. </p>

<p>On Aug. 18, a coalition of higher education groups and unions <a href="https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/desktop/document/PresidentsAllianceonHigherEducationandImmigrationetalvUnitedState?doc_id=X10FMNTJ328LAORLONP2IUNI7G">sued to block the rule</a>, arguing that requiring students to repeatedly seek federal permission to continue their studies will disrupt degree programs and make it harder for universities to recruit and retain students.</p>

<p>International students are woven into the everyday work of U.S. higher education. Making their ability to stay more dependent on repeated federal decisions will inevitably affect the institutions that rely on them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290021/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why millions of people around the world will contract measles in 2026</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754685/original/file-20260818-50-ok7zx3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=96%2C0%2C6526%2C4350&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Bangladesh has been experiencing measles outbreaks since May 2026, with more than 900 measles deaths.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/children-and-other-patients-affected-by-measles-receive-news-photo/2289576256?adppopup=true">Sony Ramani/NurPhoto via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The World Health Organization estimates that in 2026 <a href="https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/8c65dd54-ee98-4438-938c-e7114851f870/content">nearly 11 million</a> people will contract the virus that causes measles. Most of these cases will occur in Africa and Asia, but many countries in the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lana.2026.101504">Americas</a> and <a href="https://www.thinkglobalhealth.org/article/why-europe-cant-get-measles-under-control">Europe</a> are reporting outbreaks affecting hundreds or thousands of people.</p>

<p>There is no treatment for measles, but vaccines have been proven to be <a href="https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/3eb838f7-724d-41d4-9a66-47ed008deb48/content">safe and effective</a> at preventing the disease. Unvaccinated people who get sick with measles are at risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/cimb48020206">serious complications</a> that can lead to deafness, blindness and death. The risk of a <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines11081389">bad outcome</a> is higher for people who are undernourished and unable to access supportive medical care.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=IhG7428AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">infectious disease epidemiologist</a>, I study the reasons for changes in population health risks around the world. The specific factors leading to measles epidemics vary by country, but the underlying cause everywhere is decreased vaccination rates.</p>

<h2>Zero-dose children in low-income countries</h2>

<p>The vast majority of parents around the world want to protect their children from preventable infectious diseases through vaccination. In many lower-income countries, the supply of vaccines remains insufficient to meet the demand for them.</p>

<p>Because measles is highly contagious, the <a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/15-07-2026-global-childhood-immunization-coverage-inches-forward-despite-conflict-and-hesitancy---unicef--who">vaccination rate</a> needs to be above 95% to protect a community from outbreaks, creating what is known as “<a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/22599-herd-immunity">herd immunity</a>.” One dose of measles vaccine protects most people from the disease, but <a href="https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/3eb838f7-724d-41d4-9a66-47ed008deb48/content">two doses are recommended</a> to improve effectiveness.</p>

<p>Most high-income countries have measles vaccine rates near the 95% target. In Europe, the average one-dose vaccination rate is <a href="https://measles-rubella-monthly.ecdc.europa.eu/">about 94%</a>, and the two-dose rate is about 88%. In the U.S., <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm7511a2">more than 90%</a> of 2-year-olds have received at least one dose of measles vaccine and <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm7341a3">more than 92%</a> of kindergartners have received two doses. The vaccine coverage rate is above 95% in many communities, though it is much lower in some school districts.</p>

<p>In contrast, only about 80% of young children in low- and middle-income countries have received at least one dose of measles vaccine, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijid.2026.108569">only about 70%</a> have received two doses.</p>

<p>Almost every country had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21645515.2020.1804776">reduced access to vaccines</a> during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, when supply chains and clinic access were severely disrupted. Most young children in high-income countries were able to catch up on missed doses before they reached school age. But in lower-income countries, millions of kids who missed routine vaccinations during the pandemic are still classified as “<a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2026-largest-catch-up-initiative-delivers-over-100-million-childhood-vaccinations">zero-dose children</a>” who have not received any of the vaccines their countries recommend.</p>

<p>Only a tiny fraction of the cases of measles diagnosed in lower-income countries are confirmed with laboratory tests and reported to public health authorities, so it’s impossible to get an exact case count. But healthcare workers have reported observing higher than typical numbers of cases in many countries during the past year.</p>

<p>In 2026, measles epidemics have been reported in countries experiencing <a href="https://www.savethechildren.net/news/cases-measles-surge-conflict-zones-amid-vaccine-misinformation-and-cuts-international-aid">armed conflict</a> or housing refugees displaced by war, such as <a href="https://www.afro.who.int/countries/burundi/news/measles-response-intensifies-protect-refugees-burundi">Burundi</a>, <a href="https://www.doctorswithoutborders.org/latest/ebola-disease-response-continues-other-health-needs-dr-congo-must-not-be-neglected">Democratic Republic of Congo</a>, <a href="https://www.unicef.org/somalia/stories/she-watched-four-children-fall-ill">Somalia</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanmic.2026.101347">Sudan</a> and <a href="https://msfsouthasia.org/yemen-measles-threatens-children-as-families-struggle-to-reach-vaccination-and-care/">Yemen</a>.</p>

<p>Outbreaks have also been reported in peaceful countries, including <a href="https://maldivesindependent.com/society/measles-cases-rise-sixfold-in-three-weeks-as-maldives-outbreak-accelerates-949c">Maldives</a> and <a href="https://www.mwebantu.com/zambia-records-119-confirmed-measles-cases-western-province-hardest-hit/">Zambia</a>, and cases are surging in <a href="https://www.indiatoday.in/health/story/measles-cases-india-rise-26627-2026-data-gaps-elimination-target-2949312-2026-07-17">India</a>. <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/11/1166471">Dozens of other countries</a> are also experiencing epidemics. All of these situations are linked to undervaccination.</p>

<h2>Vaccine shortages in Bangladesh</h2>

<p>Bangladesh has reported more measles cases this year than any other country, and <a href="https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/struggling-measles-let-alone-much-else-4251261">more than 900 people have died</a> from the infection.</p>

<p>While Bangladesh faces many of the same challenges as other low- and middle-income countries, the past few years have presented some unique difficulties. </p>

<p>In 2024, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12115-026-01225-w">the country’s longtime government collapsed</a> and an interim government was installed. During this time of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijid.2026.108765">political instability</a> the government <a href="https://www.thinkglobalhealth.org/article/visualizing-bangladeshs-massive-measles-outbreak">ordered too few vaccine doses</a>.</p>

<p>In 2025 vaccine shortages worsened when the interim government decided to stop procuring its vaccines through UNICEF and instead tried to purchase them through a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.zs1rspw">competitive bidding process</a> before new supply chains had been established.</p>

<p>Bangladesh has now resumed working with <a href="https://www.unicef.org/stories/measles-outbreaks-child-risk">UNICEF</a> to acquire vaccines. Unfortunately, it has returned to UNICEF at a time when its partner organization <a href="https://www.gavi.org/our-work/vaccine-portfolio/measles-measles-rubella">Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance</a>, is facing funding cuts.</p>

<p>Under Gavi’s <a href="https://www.gavi.org/partner-countries/programmatic-policies/co-financing-policy">cofinancing model</a>, low- and middle-income countries’ initial vaccine purchases are subsidized by contributions from high-income countries and other investors. Over time, countries pay an increasing portion of their own vaccine costs.</p>

<p>Because Gavi pools orders from all over the world, it is able to <a href="https://www.gavi.org/our-work/market-shaping">shape markets</a> and negotiate with vaccine manufacturers for lower costs per dose. The major limitation of this system is that <a href="https://www.kff.org/global-health-policy/the-trump-administrations-foreign-aid-review-status-of-u-s-support-for-gavi-the-vaccine-alliance/">reduced funding for global health</a> shrinks the budget for subsidizing vaccine purchases.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/APo9U9SQ8_c?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The ongoing measles outbreak in Bangladesh is the result of a unique combination of political upheaval and a shortage of vaccines.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But since 2025, France, Germany, the U.K., <a href="https://theconversation.com/usaids-apparent-demise-and-the-us-withdrawal-from-who-put-millions-of-lives-worldwide-at-risk-and-imperil-us-national-security-249260">the U.S.</a> and several other high-income countries have significantly <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2025/06/cuts-in-official-development-assistance_e161f0c5/full-report.html">reduced their budgets for development assistance</a>, leaving Gavi with a substantial <a href="https://donortracker.org/publications/beyond-the-headline-gavi-6-0-pledges-in-a-constrained-funding-landscape-2026">budget shortfall</a>.</p>

<p>As Bangladesh has grown its economy, it is <a href="https://www.gavi.org/vaccineswork/50-years-progress-how-bangladesh-chose-health">paying a greater share</a> of the costs of the vaccines it purchases through Gavi. However, it does not yet have the means to fully self-finance its vaccine program. For now, if Gavi’s budget is not <a href="https://www.gavi.org/vaccineswork/50-years-progress-how-bangladesh-chose-health">fully replenished</a>, countries like Bangladesh will not have enough money to buy all of the vaccines they need.</p>

<p>Even though a <a href="https://www.unicef.org/bangladesh/en/press-releases/bangladesh-launches-emergency-measles-rubella-campaign-unicef-who-and-gavi-protect">mass vaccination campaign</a> in early 2026 saw more than 1 million Bangladeshi children vaccinated against measles, the percentage of children who have been vaccinated remains far below the 95% threshold required to prevent widespread epidemics.</p>
